planting.note: Unlike most lilies, plant bulbs shallowly with the tip just 1 inch below the soil surface, in alkaline to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; plant in early fall so the basal rosette of leaves can form and overwinter before flowering the following summer.

directions: Lilium candidum, the Madonna Lily, is one of the oldest cultivated garden flowers, depicted in Minoan frescoes and long associated with purity in Christian iconography. It produces pure white, outward-flaring trumpets with prominent gold-orange anthers and a heavy, sweet fragrance, borne in clusters of up to a dozen atop stiff stems in early to midsummer, ahead of most other lily species. Its distinctive habit of forming an autumn basal rosette of leaves that persists through winter means bulbs should be planted shallow and early, and left undisturbed for years once established, as it resents transplanting and dislikes heavy mulching over its crown. It prefers neutral to alkaline soil, unlike the acid-loving preferences of many Asiatic and Oriental hybrids.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; in zones colder than 7, mulch heavily over winter or grow in containers that can be moved to shelter, as this species is less reliably cold-hardy than most garden lily species.

directions: Lilium longiflorum, native to the Ryukyu Islands of southern Japan and Taiwan, is the classic pure white, outward-flaring trumpet lily forced into bloom for Easter and other spring holidays, though it is also a fine garden perennial in mild-winter climates. Flowers are large, waxy white, intensely fragrant, and borne a few to a stem in mid to late summer when grown outdoors on its natural schedule rather than forced. It is somewhat less cold-hardy than Asiatic or Oriental hybrids and benefits from good winter drainage and mulch protection north of zone 7. After Easter pot plants finish blooming, the bulbs can be planted out in the garden and will often re-establish and bloom again in subsequent summers.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep in acidic, humus-rich, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade with the roots kept cool; this species is intolerant of lime and benefits from staking given its very tall, heavy-flowered stems.

directions: Lilium auratum, the Goldband Lily of Japan, produces some of the largest flowers of any lily species: huge, outward-facing white bowls up to 10 inches across, each petal marked with a bold golden-yellow central stripe and scattered crimson spots, and carrying an intense, heady fragrance. It blooms in late summer on tall stems that can reach 6 feet, often bearing a dozen or more flowers per stem in vigorous, well-established clumps. Introduced to the West in the 1860s, it caused a sensation and became a foundational parent species behind the modern Oriental hybrid lily group, including cultivars like Casa Blanca and Stargazer. It requires acidic soil and excellent drainage, and is shorter-lived in gardens than its hybrid descendants, but remains prized by species-lily collectors.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; late emergence in spring is normal for this species, so mark planting locations to avoid accidental disturbance.

directions: Lilium speciosum, the Japanese Lily, bears strongly reflexed, Turk's-cap-like flowers in shades of white to deep pink, heavily overlaid with raised crimson spots and papillae, and carries a rich, classic lily fragrance. It blooms notably late, from late summer into early fall, extending the lily season after most Asiatic and early Oriental types have finished. Along with L. auratum, it is one of the principal wild parents of the modern Oriental hybrid lily group, passing on fragrance, recurved petal form, and late bloom timing to cultivars such as Sorbonne and Muscadet. It prefers cool, acidic, humus-rich soil with reliable moisture and appreciates light shade from hot afternoon sun in warmer zones.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; this mountain-meadow species tolerates a wide range of soil pH and is among the easiest and most cold-hardy of the true lily species.

directions: Lilium bulbiferum, the Orange Lily or Fire Lily, is a European mountain-meadow species bearing clusters of upright, unspotted, cup-shaped orange-red flowers in early to midsummer, earlier than most other lily species. It is unscented but valued for its vivid color, cold hardiness, and easy garden temperament, thriving from the Alps down through naturalized populations in the British Isles, where the var. croceum form is a well-known wildflower. The species name refers to var. bulbiferum's habit of producing small dark bulbils in the leaf axils, which drop and root to slowly naturalize a clump or patch. It is a good choice for rock gardens, cottage borders, and cold-climate gardens where more tender lily species struggle.

planting.note: Plant small bulbs 3-4 inches deep in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; this diminutive steppe species is well suited to rock gardens and the front of borders and is one of the easiest lily species to raise from seed, often flowering in its second year.

directions: Lilium pumilum, the Coral Lily, is a diminutive species native to the steppes and open woodlands of Siberia, Mongolia, Korea, and northern China, bearing small, nodding, brilliant scarlet Turk's-cap flowers with strongly reflexed petals and a light, sweet fragrance carried on wiry, grass-thin stems. It is among the most cold-hardy and easiest lily species to grow from seed, often blooming in as little as two years, and its short stature makes it a natural fit for rock gardens, gravel plantings, and the front of a sunny border where taller hybrid lilies would overwhelm it. Its brilliant, unspotted red color and airy habit set it apart from the larger-flowered, heavier hybrid groups.

common_name: Scheherazade Lily (Tall Orienpet Hybrid with Deep Burgundy-Red, Gold-Edged Reflexed Petals)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; provide sturdy staking or grow against a wall or fence for wind protection, as flowering stems can reach 7-8 feet and become top-heavy with a dozen or more large blooms.

directions: 'Scheherazade' is a landmark Orienpet (OT) hybrid bred by Judith Freeman, crossing Oriental and Trumpet lily lines to combine the vigor and heat tolerance of trumpet species with the flower form and fragrance of Orientals. Huge, outward-facing flowers open deep burgundy-maroon at the petal base shading to a wide cream-gold margin at the tip, with darker spotting through the throat, and carry a strong, sweet fragrance. Stems are exceptionally tall and robust, commonly reaching 6 to 8 feet in good soil, and a single mature bulb can produce a dozen or more flowers in a candelabra-like head in midsummer. It is markedly more heat- and disease-tolerant than pure Oriental hybrids, making it a favorite for southern and hot-summer gardens as well as northern ones.

common_name: Navona Lily (Pure White Fragrant LA Hybrid Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; sturdy stems generally need no staking, making this a reliable choice for borders and cutting gardens alike.

directions: 'Navona' is a widely grown LA hybrid, part of the group bred by crossing Longiflorum (Easter Lily) lines with Asiatic hybrids to combine trumpet-lily flower size and form with Asiatic vigor, sturdiness, and a broader color and bloom-time range. It bears large, outward-facing to slightly upturned, pure white flowers with a faint creamy throat blush and only mild fragrance, opening in early to midsummer ahead of most Oriental hybrids. Stems are strong and self-supporting, and the flowers hold up exceptionally well as cut stems, which has made 'Navona' a staple of both the cut-flower trade and home perennial borders. It multiplies readily and is a dependable, low-maintenance choice for growers who want lily impact without the taller Orienpet or Oriental hybrids' extra height and staking needs.

common_name: Black Out Lily (Upward-Facing Near-Black Deep Red Asiatic Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this compact Asiatic hybrid is unscented and needs no staking, making it a low-maintenance choice for beds, borders, and containers.

directions: 'Black Out' is a popular Asiatic hybrid lily prized for its unusually dark, near-black deep maroon-red flowers, which open upward-facing in tight, star-shaped clusters atop sturdy, compact stems. Like other Asiatic hybrids it is unscented but blooms reliably in midsummer, is easy to grow, multiplies quickly into full clumps, and requires no staking even in exposed sites, making it one of the more forgiving lilies for beginning gardeners. Its dramatically dark color makes it a striking accent against pale companions such as white phlox, silver artemisia, or light-colored daylilies, and it is widely offered by mainstream bulb retailers as a garden and cut-flower lily.
